sources.news_title: US proposes tariffs on trade partners, including China
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump fired a new tariff salvo on Wednesday on 14 major trading partners including China, Japan and the European Union, undeterred in his protectionist push by the losses his Republican Party suffered in US midterm elections.
His administration proposed new maximum potential rates of 20 percent to 40 percent to counter excess industrial capacity that it says these countries are promoting. But the US Trade Representative's office said it intends to cap new tariffs at lower levels agreed under trade deals that are completed or still under negotiation.
In unveiling the results of an eight-month unfair trade practices investigation into excess industrial capacity, USTR aims to more fully rebuild Trump's tariff leverage after the Supreme Court in February struck down his broad global duties under a national emergencies law.
Under the excess factory capacity probe, USTR said China would face the highest capped rate of 20 percent, which would be added to duties of roughly 25 percent imposed during Trump's first term.
That rate would comply with a US-China trade truce that expires on January 10. But if the truce unravels, China's rate would rise to 40 percent, the USTR said.
Vietnam would face a capped tariff rate of 20 percent if it reaches a trade agreement with Washington, rising to 35 percent if negotiations fail.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the tariffs, which would not take effect until after a January 25 public hearing, were intended to counteract "industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labour suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices" that undermine the US manufacturing base.
The duties would not stack on top of prior tariffs of 10 percent or 12.5 percent imposed under a separate US probe into allegedly lax enforcement of anti-forced labour laws in 60 economies, nor would they add to sectoral national security duties on steel, aluminium, autos and other goods.
Greer said the proposed tariffs also would not apply to about US$30 billion of Chinese imports under consideration for tariff reductions through a bilateral mechanism known as the Board of Trade.
Washington has long accused China of subsidising industry and flooding global markets with low-cost exports ranging from steel to electric vehicles and solar products.
A spokesperson for China's embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China is a source of excess capacity.
"The so-called issue of 'industrial overcapacity' does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation," the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements between President Xi Jinping and Trump.
Speaking before the new tariffs were announced, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said tariff wars and trade wars serve no one's interests, adding that both sides should resolve economic and trade issues through consultation on the basis of equality, respect and mutual benefit. 
The USTR also proposed capped tariff rates of 18 percent for imported goods from Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Bangladesh, and 15 percent, including existing "Most Favoured Nation" duties, for Japan, South Korea, the EU and Switzerland.
India, which has yet to reach a trade deal with the Trump administration, would face a 17 percent tariff rate if an agreement is finalised and a 25 percent rate if talks fail, the USTR said. Singapore would receive a capped tariff rate of 10 percent.
Mexico and Norway were excluded from the proposals because investigations into their trade practices remain under way, Greer said.
Separately, USTR proposed a new 10 percent tariff on imports of Brazil's finished Embraer commercial aircraft, and an increase in duties on imports of Brazilian sugar that exceed quotas as part of an effort to push Brasilia to rectify alleged unfair trade practices.
The products were previously exempted from Trump's 25 percent tariffs on Brazilian goods that were imposed in July under a separate Section 301 investigation. Greer said he decided to propose the tariff increases after months of talks between the US and Brazil made "no meaningful progress." (Reuters/ Xinhua)

sources.news_title: Tariff Man Strikes Again
sources.text:
Tariff Man Strikes Again
The Trump administration unveils new proposed tariffs on 14 economies, from China to the European Union.
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at new proposed U.S. tariffs on China and other trade partners, tensions between Ukraine and Libya over a drone attack, and the end of a long deportation battle in the United States.
World Brief will be off Thursday and Friday for the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday. We will return on Monday, Nov. 30.
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at new proposed U.S. tariffs on China and other trade partners, tensions between Ukraine and Libya over a drone attack, and the end of a long deportation battle in the United States.
World Brief will be off Thursday and Friday for the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday. We will return on Monday, Nov. 30.
Excess Capacity
The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed a fresh batch of tariffs on more than a dozen major trading partners, including China, Japan, South Korea, and the European Union.
The proposed tariff rates, which could be implemented early next year, range from 15 percent for the EU, Taiwan, and South Korea, 18 percent for most others, and rates of as much as 25 percent on India or 35 percent on Vietnam. China faces a fresh tariff rate of 20 percent, which will be stacked on top of duties still lingering from U.S. President Donald Trump’s first term—and that’s only if the trade truce between Beijing and Washington holds. (It expires in January.)
The latest tariffs are the culmination of an investigation launched this spring into alleged excess industrial capacity among nearly all U.S. trading partners. U.S. trade officials allege that other countries artificially prop up their manufacturing sectors with subsidies, promotions, tax breaks, and other measures that distort trade and disadvantage U.S. exports. U.S. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has taken equity stakes in dozens of private companies and is actively promoting state involvement in the manufacture of everything from chips to ships.
China’s Foreign Ministry said the new tariffs are based on a “false proposition,” though China is one of the few countries among the 14 economies targeted that demonstrates genuine excess capacity that is harming the U.S. and global economies. Even trade specialists who are skeptical of the Trump administration’s affinity for tariffs believe that higher duties on Chinese exports are warranted.
The European Commission also hit back at the tariffs, arguing that Europe is a victim of overcapacity, not a source of the problem.
The Trump administration is using Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act to levy the new duties—the same law that it used earlier this year to slap tariffs on 60 economies on the grounds that they do not adequately police forced labor in their supply chains. (Those tariffs were challenged in court.) The proposed new tariffs would essentially replace (and slightly raise) the rates levied earlier, implying that the question of forced labor has been solved in just a few months.
The measures proposed on Wednesday are just the latest attempt by the Trump administration to find a formula to recreate in the aggregate the sweeping global tariffs that the U.S. Supreme Court struck down earlier this year. The administration has used at least four different trade authorities dating back almost a century to continue raising barriers to trade, despite polls showing that the widespread unpopularity of tariffs contributed to the Republicans’ historic midterm election wipeout.
Today’s Most Read
- Huang’s Return Is the Biggest National Security Scandal in U.S. History by James Palmer
- Spinning Genocide by Suzy Hansen
- The Middle East Is Finally on Its Own by Stephen M. Walt
What We’re Following
Toxic explosives. The U.S. Army on Wednesday blew up nearly five tons of toxic lead explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. The intentional detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide, a sensitive chemical compound used by the military in explosives, was originally scheduled to take place last Friday. The controlled explosion was delayed, however, amid public pushback and legal challenges from environmental groups.
Destroying the bomb-making material, which had been stored in the Iowa plant since 2009, was deemed necessary by the military after inspectors in March discovered that it had partially crystallized—increasing the risk of a spontaneous explosion. But the plan to detonate the material raised concerns over the potential for toxic lead dust to spread over a large area, and many locals also said they weren’t given enough notice to prepare.
Residents within five miles of the blast were urged to evacuate ahead of the detonation, while others in the vicinity were told to remain indoors.
After the detonation, the Environmental Protection Agency wrote on X that its real-time air monitors were reporting “ZERO detection of airborne lead throughout the region.” Adam Telle, the Army’s acting secretary, also wrote on X that the “controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success” and said the threat of an “uncontrolled spontaneous detonation has been eliminated.”
Ukraine and Libya. Kyiv has seemingly angered the primary military force in eastern Libya, the Libyan National Army (LNA), after attacking a Russian warship that was refueling at the Benghazi Naval Base on Sunday. Two Libyan naval officers died from wounds sustained in the Ukrainian sea drone attack. The LNA has vowed to retaliate “at the appropriate time and place, and by the appropriate means.”
Ukraine offered no immediate public response on Wednesday, though officials said the previous day that Ukrainian forces hadn’t targeted Libyans in the operation.
The incident is yet another example of how the Russia-Ukraine war has spread to other parts of the globe. Russian missiles crashed in Poland last week, and there have been repeated Russian drone incursions on NATO’s eastern flank. Ukraine also carried out a drone attack on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland this past weekend.
A ‘free man.’ Kilmar Abrego Garcia arrived in Spain on Wednesday as part of a negotiated agreement between the Salvadoran immigrant’s attorneys and the U.S. government after a prolonged, highly publicized deportation battle with the Trump administration. “I’m happy, and I’m celebrating my freedom,” Abrego Garcia told reporters in Spanish after he landed.
Amid the administration’s controversial crackdown on immigration, Abrego Garcia was arrested last year by federal agents in Maryland, wrongfully deported, and placed in a notorious prison in El Salvador before he was ultimately brought back to the United States. The Trump administration continued to target Abrego Garcia for deportation and aimed to send him to Liberia, but that was blocked by the courts.
Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, an attorney for Abrego Garcia, said that his client left the United States a “free man” and signaled that Abrego Garcia would attempt to return once Trump is no longer in office. “Kilmar Abrego Garcia is going to outlast Donald Trump, and he’ll be back in the United States as a lawful permanent resident,” he said.
Odds and Ends
On Wednesday, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali became the first Pakistani national to reach orbit and the first foreign astronaut to board China’s Tiangong space station. Ali, who will return to Earth in a few days, told reporters that he carries “the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis.” We officially feel like underachievers.

New Trump Tariffs — Nice
Following an election in which voters responded in historic fashion to rising prices — due mostly to Trump’s tariffs and Trump’s war on Iran — President Donald Trump has decided to jack up prices even further by launching a series of new tariffs. The new tariffs span 14 countries or other trading partners.
First of all, the big names here are China and the European Union. As if the prices of all kinds of goods haven’t gone up enough, Trump decided to raise the tariffs on Chinese products from about 20% to about 40%. Don’t expect importers and retailers to eat those costs. Those will certainly be passed on to consumers, even if not fully.
The tariff on products produced in the EU is 15%, which is exactly the maximum tariff agreed to in a 2025 negotiation between the US and the EU. I imagine the EU didn’t anticipate the US turning around and implementing the maximum tariff a year later….
In addition to China and Europe, Trump added tariffs onto products produced in Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, and Vietnam.
“The administration is now using section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 as the legal basis for the new rounds of tariffs. The law gives the executive branch power to respond to unfair foreign trade practices after conducting formal investigations,” The Guardian reports. “Though the White House did not give a timeline for the new tariffs, it said they could go into effect in January at the earliest. The US trade office said it would hold hearings on the new tariffs and its investigation into the unfair trade practices on 25 January.”
It looks like Trump and team are happy to keep jacking up prices on US consumer goods into 2027, even just after the total blue tsunami that just swept the nation. It seems that Trump just doesn’t care, and is stuck in a 1970s-era ideology around the economy, trade, and tariffs. And we’ll all pay the price for that.
Happy Thanksgiving!

THE UNITED STATES has announced another wave of proposed tariffs today on 14 economies including the European Union and China.
The duties, proposed at up to 20%, come over allegations the economies “are promoting production and capacity divorced from the realities of demand and market principles,” a senior US official said on condition of anonymity.
This is the latest move by US president Donald Trump to remake Washington’s trade relationships after a months-long probe into alleged excess production.
The new tariffs face a period of public comment before taking effect, with the official adding that the proposals take existing trade deals into account.
The new levies target some of the largest US trading partners, including China, the European Union, India, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.
The EU has said that it rejected the premise of new tariffs on its exports proposed by the United States and expected Washington to stick by a deal struck with Brussels last year.
A 20% tariff is being proposed for China, the joint-highest for any economy, but US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new levies were within the bounds of existing trade negotiations with Beijing.
“China understands that we’re going to have some level of tariffs. This falls within that understanding,” he told US broadcaster CNBC on Wednesday, adding that the United States was also offering China exemptions on around $30 billion (€27.43 billion) of goods.
Earlier, however, China’s foreign ministry warned Washington not to engage in “tariff wars and trade wars,” responding to a question about the new levies, which had not yet been announced at the time.
Vietnam also faces a proposed 20-percent tariff; Cambodia and Indonesia 18%; and India 17%, according to the USTR’s office.
Partners like the EU, Korea and Taiwan, which have signed earlier trade deals, will see tariffs broadly capped at 15%.
In a separate announcement, USTR also proposed additional tariffs on goods from Brazil, including aircraft, over alleged inaction on addressing US trade concerns.
Trump’s tariffs have targeted Washington’s friends and foes alike, and are part of a push in his second term to remake global trade by forcing countries to buy US products or produce their goods in his country.
The new tariffs could raise temperatures as the US president prepares to host G20 leaders in Miami in December.
“We don’t expect this to create tension or rancor” at the G20 summit, the senior US official said. “We actually expect that we may be signing more agreements at the G20 in the wake of these announcements.”
Over-capacity concerns affect a range of sectors, from batteries to cement, chemicals to processed food, the senior US official said.
The duties could add further pressure on US businesses already squeezed by earlier tariffs, with firms now likelier to pass on costs to consumers already frustrated with the high cost of living.
Affordability was a key issue in recent midterm elections, which saw Trump’s Republican Party swept out of power in both houses of Congress by Democrats.
The US Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge came in at a three-year high in October, as prices are pushed up by the effects of Trump’s war on Iran, tariffs, and the massive AI investment boom.
Fed policymakers, responsible for keeping inflation to a long-term two-percent target, say that most price effects of Trump’s previous tariff rollout have passed through the economy – but any new levies could push prices up further.
The new tariffs are likely to come into effect in January at the earliest, the senior US official said.
The USTR began its investigation on excess manufacturing capacity and production in March, days after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s previous slew of tariffs.
Trade lawyer Ryan Majerus told AFP that he expected this probe to be among “the most important” actions for the Trump administration, given its underlying concern that factories with excess capacity start operations abroad and “never get turned off, even if there’s no demand.”
This potentially leads to an oversupply of goods, depressed prices and a “hollowing out” of US manufacturing, he added.
While the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s global tariffs in February, his sector-specific duties remain intact.
The new tariffs will not stack on top of those sector-specific tariffs on items like automobiles and steel, the senior US official said.
In July, Trump imposed a separate wave of tariffs on 60 economies, accusing them of insufficient action against forced labour.
For economies facing both the forced labour and excess production tariffs, the levies would not stack, the US official said. Instead, the higher rate of the two would prevail.

sources.news_title: Trump administration proposes new round of tariffs, raising risks of price hikes across Texas
sources.text:
The Trump administration is recommending new tariffs of up to 20% on 14 major U.S. trading partners, including China, the European Union, Japan, and South Korea.
U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer alleged unfair trade practices as the reason for proposing new tariffs under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
"For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America's manufacturing base," Greer said. "But where successive statements at the G7, G20, WTO and other fora have not resulted in change, President Trump is proposing to take action to bring about the elimination of these unfair acts, policies, and practices."
The Office of the USTR added, "The Trade Representative has not made determinations with respect to Mexico or Norway at this time," suggesting additional Section 301 tariffs are still on the table.
The proposed tariffs will have to go through a public comment period, but Dallas-based trade lawyer Michelle Schulz expects them to be approved.
"My understanding is that the USTR and Department of Commerce have already looked at this extensively," Schulz said.So they have written a substantial report that they will use to back up their claims that there are unfair trade practices."
Texas is the nation's leading state for trade. That makes it the most exposed to the effects of tariffs. The new tariffs, if approved, would put further upward pressure on prices for Texas businesses and consumers, on top of that imposed by earlier tariffs applied by the Trump administration.
"We have a lot of companies here in Texas who are manufacturing, whether it’s just parts and components or it’s machinery," Schulz said. "Those companies have had to increase their prices because the components that they import can’t be obtained elsewhere, they can’t be made here, or at least not quickly."
While the U.S. International Court of Trade forced the Trump administration to drop tariffs it had applied to most major U.S. trading partners utilizing the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, other tariffs it applied using Section 301 remain in force.
Kacie Wright manages Houghton Horns, a brass instrument specialty shop north of Fort Worth. The business sells student instruments made in China and professional-quality instruments made in Germany and Japan; all would be affected by the proposed new tariffs.
“For November 2024 [Black Friday] we did $279,000 in online sales," Wright said. "For November 2025 we did $92,000 in sales. Higher tariffs means higher prices, which will depress those numbers even further.”
Otaku Café is also bracing for fresh pain. The combination hobby store and video game arcade in San Antonio imports most of what it sells from China or Japan.
"It’s hit pretty hard. And I don’t mean just for us personally, in my own business. It’s the people in our industry," said Richard Giron, Otaku Café's co-owner. "We’re not the only [hobby] store in town, and others have closed during this time because of the past two years."
Houghton Horns and Otaku Café are two of more than 1,000 U.S. small businesses working through a coalition called We Pay the Tariffs, that have signed a joint letter to the leaders of the next Congress requesting tariff relief as a means of combating high prices.
“Three weeks ago, voters unambiguously rejected tariffs that have worsened the affordability crisis and devastated small businesses. Customers can't afford more price increases, but small businesses can't afford to absorb tariffs on top of tariffs either," said Dan Anthony, executive director of We Pay the Tariffs. "Congress must listen to voters and end these tariffs immediately.”

Was David Jones Hornsby losing $4 million a year?
During her interview on 2GB today David Jones chief executive Erica Berchtold seemed to confirm reports that the Hornsby store in Sydney's north was losing up to $4 million a year, while others made large profits.
She said Sydney's metro had made it easier to visit the upgraded store at Chatswood and historic city store, but changing demographics in the area was also a factor.
When asked why a loss-making store remained open so long she said:
"It's hard to make those decisions. you've got to work with your landlords and try and negotiate your way out of that."
As to the broader reason for the department chain's collapse, she said it was a "perfect storm of everything".
"Sure, you've got an online business growing. You've also got changing customer demographics. I mean, we've been around for 188 years. Some of the leases that we've got on stores are 20, 30-year leases, right? Things change, right?
"And customers behavior changes. And I just don't think we moved quickly enough to adapt to that change and make sure we were reshaping the business, looking at external factors, getting ahead of them, and doing the reset and the hard decisions that needed to be made."
She also confirmed extra roles from their support roles and among the executive would also go.
"I can't talk about what happened in the past, but unfortunately now we've had to make some really hard decisions from the top down.
Also confirmed were reports of other retailers reaching out to offer places to floor staff made redundant.
"The retail industry is such a wonderful industry to work in and we have had so many other retailers reaching out wanting to redeploy David Jones team members because they know we've got really hardworking, dedicated, experienced team members," she said.
"That's even some of our competitors reaching out for that. So, thank you to all of our fellow retailers."

David Jones boss confirms she said past management 'did not have the balls'
Still on David Jones chief executive Erica Berchtold's interview with 2GB, she confirmed reports that she had told others that past management "did not have the balls to make tough decisions".
"Oh gosh, that's bold. I probably have said something like that, so I think I'd have to say true," Ms Berchtold said in a game of true or false with host Ben Fordham.
The former chief commercial officer for the department store said when she took the reins of the company about a year ago, she knew it was in trouble and needed an immediate plan to save the icon.
"My reaction was, geez, we better come up with a plan and move fast," she said.
"So come on, let's act. Let's reinvent and let's go."
She said she could see all the external pressures facing the retail chain.
"We need to lift our game a little bit more because I think we rested on our laurels or on our heritage and actually customers are telling us: 'We've loved you in the past, we're really rooting for you now, but please could you give us what we need?'"
Customers were also encouraged to make use of the Black Friday sales and Ms Berchtold scotched rumors its shelves were empty.
"We have been buying more stock through this whole process. So, we are not empty.
"Don't believe all those rubbish stories that you've seen online where someone's gone in and taken a photo of one little empty shelf and said that's what the whole store looks like.
"That is absolute rubbish. Come in, support us, and see us through this because we're going to reinvent ourselves for the future."
David Jones expects a buyer in the new year
David Jones chief executive Erica Berchtold has told Sydney's 2GB radio that the company expects to find a buyer for the troubled department store early in the new year.
Speaking to host Ben Fordham, she said she wanted the DJs team, suppliers and customers to know that "we have a really great plan for the business".
"It's really unfortunate the situation we find ourselves in at the moment. But we have a plan and we're heading towards that still even in these difficult times," she said.
"It's really going to depend on who wants to buy the business and there is a lot of interest, a lot of varying parties that are looking at the business, and it's really going to be up to how many stores they would like to take forward.
"The administrators are managing the sale of the business and so I am preparing the materials.
"As soon as we find a new buyer, and that'll be early in the new year, I would hope, that we will have a new buyer of the business and we will take that forward and off we go."
Key Event
Flight Centre investigating cybersecurity incident
Flight Centre has told the market that it is investigating "unusual activity in a third-party accommodation booking system" used by some of its leisure travel brands.
In an ASX statement, the company said unusual activity had been detected in the accommodation system used by Flight Centre brand Travel Associates, Cruiseabout and some independent agents.
"While investigations remain ongoing, at this stage Flight Centre believes that a significant number of customer records in the impacted system may have been accessed by unknown persons, although it is not clear at this time how many of those records have actually been extracted from the third-party system," it said.
The initial review indicated that most of the accessed records contain customer names, some with basic travel information, the company said.
"A very small percentage is believed to include data such as limited passport details, email addresses, phone numbers, birth dates, or in rare cases health or mobility information.
"To date, no access to customer credit card, payment or bank account details has been identified."

Australian superannuation pool hits $4.7t in September quarter
Australia's total superannuation assets rose 0.3%q/q in the September quarter to $4.7 trillion, according to the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA)'s quarterly report.

The US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter, while inflation increased further in October, reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise rates next month and again in early 2027.
Markets fully expect a rate hike at the Fed's December policy meeting and price in a 60% chance of a larger, 50-basis-point increase in January, according to CME's FedWatch tool. The central bank last raised rates in September.

Are these tariffs legal?
Not all of them.
Under the US Constitution, Congress has power over the purse, meaning it has sole responsibility for taxes — including tariffs.
Mr Trump tried to find a way to give himself authority by declaring two national emergencies, which he argued allowed him to introduce "emergency tariffs".
The Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS) struck that move down in February, but other tariffs, which Mr Trump implemented under different legislation, stayed in place.

sources.news_title: Trump Proposes Section 301 Tariffs of Up to 20% on 14 Trading Partners to Address Industrial Overcapacity
sources.text:
There’s a sound that haunts the small towns of Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Michigan – the silence of a factory floor that used to hum. For decades, American manufacturing has been bled dry by foreign competitors who don’t play by the same rules. Governments in Beijing, Brussels, and beyond pour subsidies into their industries, then flood global markets with cheap goods that no American plant can match on price alone.
The scope of the problem is staggering. We’re not just talking about steel anymore – though that’s bad enough. Batteries, cement, chemicals, processed food. Entire sectors where state-backed foreign producers churn out more than the world could possibly absorb, crushing prices and the American workers who used to make those things. China’s trade surplus has ballooned to record highs, and nobody in Washington should be pretending that’s an accident. As one trade lawyer put it to AFP, these subsidized factories “never get turned off, even if there’s no demand.” The result? Oversupply, depressed prices, and a hollowed-out industrial base right here at home.
When the Supreme Court struck down President Trump’s emergency tariffs last February, critics couldn’t pop the champagne fast enough. They assumed the trade fight was over. They didn’t bother reading the fine print. The administration launched a formal Section 301 investigation in March – a methodical, legally grounded probe into unfair trade practices – and on Wednesday, it delivered its answer.
New tariffs, new legal footing
The White House proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, targeting the structural overcapacity that has tilted the playing field against American manufacturers for years.
From Reuters:
“We know that they don’t like these actions, but we are seeking stability with the Chinese. China is seeking stability with us,” a senior US official said, adding Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping last week was “really great.” Even so, as ING analysts noted, “while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind.”
Behind the diplomatic language, the numbers tell a straightforward story. China faces the highest proposed rate at 20%. The EU, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, India, Vietnam, and eight other economies are also in the crosshairs. Critically, the new duties won’t exceed caps already negotiated in existing trade deals – 20% for China, 15% for the EU and Japan, 19% for Malaysia. They also won’t stack on top of the forced-labor tariffs imposed on 60 countries in July; whichever rate is higher prevails.
Specific rates will be published in the Federal Register, with a public comment period and hearing before implementation – likely no earlier than January.
The price of doing nothing
Look, I’m not going to pretend these tariffs are painless. Inflation sits at 3.7%. Republicans just got hammered in the midterms. A Reuters/Ipsos poll shows 62% of Americans want tariffs repealed. The media loves that number. You’ll see it in every headline for the next two weeks.
But funny how nobody polls the follow-up question: what happens when we can’t make our own cement? Our own batteries? When every critical supply chain runs through a country that views us as a strategic competitor?
Short-term price increases are real. I feel them at the grocery store like everyone else. But long-term dependence on foreign rivals who subsidize their industries as a matter of national strategy? That’s not an inconvenience – that’s an existential threat.
The factory floor doesn’t have to stay quiet. Whether this administration – now staring down a Democratic Congress with no appetite for trade fights – has the spine to see it through is the only question that actually matters.
Key Takeaways
- Trump proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners to counter foreign overcapacity threatening American manufacturing.
- China faces the highest proposed rate at 20%; duties won’t exceed existing trade deal caps.
- New tariffs use Section 301 legal authority after the Supreme Court struck down emergency tariffs in February.
- Short-term consumer costs are real, but long-term industrial dependence on rivals poses a far greater threat.

The United Kingdom was never among the 16 economies investigated from March, and it is not among the 14 now in Washington’s sights.
“For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America’s manufacturing base,” Greer said.
The EU faces a proposed 15 percent, or up to 20 percent if Washington judges Brussels’s existing commitments unsatisfactory. China faces up to 20 percent, India up to 25 percent, and Vietnam up to 35 percent, with lower rates on offer to countries that strike trade agreements. Singapore faces up to 20 percent; Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand face up to 18 percent; and Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Switzerland face up to 15 percent. Mexico and Norway, also investigated, have yet to receive a decision.
Washington’s charge sheet against Brussels includes industrial plans to expand manufacturing, export credits that prop up production, barriers to American goods, cheap loans from state-backed investment banks, and a failure to tackle global overcapacity, including imports and investment from non-market economies such as China. The car, chemicals, and pharmaceutical industries are singled out.
Another Brexit Benefit?
Inside the EU, Britain would have had no say. Trade policy, including tariffs, is an exclusive power of the bloc, and Washington has targeted the EU as a single unit, covering “all goods of the EU,” not individual member states. If Britain were still inside, it would almost certainly have been subject to the same tariffs.
The timing is awkward for Prime Minister Burnham. On November 20, his government and the EU concluded a deal on food and farming standards that will work on the basis of “dynamic alignment,” with “the UK and EU applying the same rules, at the same time, on an ongoing basis,” from March 1, 2028. In practice, this will amount to the British government adopting EU regulations, enforced by EU judges. Burnham told the summit in Brussels on November 20 that legislation to implement the deal, along with a link to the EU’s carbon trading scheme, would go before Parliament the following week.
The National Pulse reported last week that the one EU demand Burnham is resisting is matching the bloc’s tariffs on Chinese goods, even as he signs up to its food rules, carbon trading, and a youth migration scheme. His wider timetable for drawing Britain back towards Brussels now runs into an American administration preparing to tariff the very bloc he is courting.

sources.news_title: US Targets 14 Economies With New Overcapacity Tariffs
sources.text:
The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China, the European Union, Japan, South Korea and India, accusing them of fueling global industrial overcapacity, in its latest move to rebuild a tariff wall that the Supreme Court partly dismantled earlier this year.
The proposal follows an eight-month investigation by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which originally covered 16 economies. A senior U.S. official said tariffs were proposed on goods from China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.
Mexico and Norway, the other two economies under investigation, were left off the list for now. The official said USTR was still reviewing its excess-capacity findings on the two countries and declined to give a timeline for completing that review.
Washington concluded that each of the 14 partners "creates, sustains, or contributes to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors through various acts, policies, and practices that we find to be unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce," the official said.
USTR defines structural excess capacity as situations where countries "are promoting production and capacity divorced from the realities of demand and market principles," according to the official, citing industrial policies, government subsidies and the use of components imported from non-market economies. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, who opened the probe in March, has argued that subsidies and other state support have allowed foreign producers to flood world markets with cheap goods and undercut American manufacturers.
China faces the steepest proposed duty. The plan calls for a 20% excess-capacity tariff on Chinese goods, on top of the roughly 25% tariffs imposed during Trump's first term. Vietnam, which has absorbed a large share of manufacturing investment that moved out of China in recent years, was also proposed at 20%.
For close U.S. allies with existing trade deals, the official said the new duties would stay within the tariff caps already agreed. That means a ceiling of 15% for the European Union, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, and 19% for Malaysia. Rates for the remaining partners were set to be published in a Federal Register notice on Wednesday.
The new duties will not be added on top of everything else. They would not stack on the 10% or 12.5% tariffs the administration imposed in July on 60 economies over what it called inadequate enforcement of bans on goods made with forced labor; where both apply, the higher rate would prevail. They also would not stack on sector-specific tariffs, such as those on autos and steel.
About $30 billion in Chinese imports now under review for tariff reductions through a bilateral "Board of Trade" process would be exempt, the official said.
The measures are proposals, not final duties. They must go through a public notice period, a comment period and a hearing before taking effect, and the official said implementation could slip into January. That timing lines up with a separate deadline: the U.S.-China trade truce, reached in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025, is set to expire on Jan. 10.
The official said the administration does not expect Beijing to retaliate, describing both sides as "seeking stability," and called President Donald Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping last week "really great." The official also pointed to progress on Chinese supplies of rare earth minerals, a key point of leverage for Beijing in past rounds of the trade fight.
China has long rejected the overcapacity charge. When Washington launched the investigation in March, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun called so-called overcapacity "a false proposition" and said Beijing opposed using it as a pretext for political manipulation. In July, China's Commerce Ministry issued a report arguing that its export strength reflects competitiveness rather than excess production, and said the United States had no authority to unilaterally label its trading partners' output as excess capacity.
Washington accuses China of flooding global markets with steel, aluminum, electric vehicles, solar products, appliances and other manufactured goods, often at prices below those of Western competitors. Surging exports pushed China's trade surplus to a record of nearly $1.2 trillion last year. Part of the U.S. probe also targets Chinese investment in Southeast Asian factories, which the administration sees as a route for Chinese firms to avoid American tariffs by shipping from third countries.
The official suggested the proposed duties could speed up negotiations with partners that have not yet finalized trade agreements with the United States, including India and Vietnam, and said more deals could be reached around the Group of 20 leaders' summit in Miami in December.
Brazil, which was not part of the overcapacity probe, was singled out separately on Wednesday after trade talks stalled. The United States proposed higher duties on raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a step that would hit Brazilian planemaker Embraer. Washington imposed a 25% tariff on a broad range of Brazilian goods in July, though aircraft and aircraft parts were exempted at the time.
The new proposals are part of a broader effort by the administration to restore its tariff program after the Supreme Court in February struck down Trump's sweeping global tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. Trump responded with a temporary 10% global tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act, then replaced it in July with the forced labor duties of up to 12.5% on 60 economies under Section 301. Trade analysts widely view the July duties and the new overcapacity proposals as a rebuild of the tariffs the court invalidated, this time on a legal footing that relies on country-by-country investigations rather than emergency powers.
Section 301 has a longer track record in court. It was the basis for the tariffs Trump imposed on Chinese goods during his first term, many of which were kept in place by the Biden administration, and it requires USTR to document unfair practices and take public input before acting. That process is slower than an emergency order, but it gives the duties firmer legal ground if they are challenged.
The proposals come at a politically sensitive moment for the White House. Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress in this month's midterm elections, and a national poll conducted after the vote found 62% of respondents would support efforts to repeal the tariffs. U.S. consumer inflation stood at 3.7% year on year in September, and Federal Reserve policymakers have warned that new levies could push prices higher.
For allies such as South Korea, Japan and the European Union, the immediate impact may be limited because the proposed rates fall within ceilings they already negotiated. But the move adds a new legal basis for those tariffs, after the court ruling had cast doubt on the authority behind them, and keeps pressure on governments that are still bargaining with Washington.
The administration said congressional committees have been briefed and that all 14 trading partners have been notified of the proposed actions. The Federal Register notice is expected to set out country-by-country rates, the products covered and the deadlines for public comment, which will determine how quickly the duties can take effect.

sources.news_title: U.S. plans to hike tariffs on China, EU, Brazil and others over subsidized production
sources.text: WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration announced a set of broad new tariffs Wednesday on imports from China, the European Union, Taiwan and 11 other countries in response to their alleged overproduction of factory goods that have disadvantaged American firms. The new tariffs are also intended to help replace the revenue lost after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in February that U.S. President Donald Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs. Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative, told CNBC that many U.S. trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base.” The proposed duties range from 15 per cent to 35 per cent and could cover roughly three-fifths of U.S. imports, though the administration also proposed exemptions for products such as semiconductors and other high-tech goods from Taiwan and South Korea, which are crucial to the artificial intelligence buildout. While sweeping, the tariffs largely replace those first imposed last April and should have a modest impact on inflation and growth, economists said. The duties “were widely expected, are relatively small, and would return us roughly to where we were earlier in the year,” Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics, said. Yet the announcement demonstrates the Trump administration’s willingness to continue imposing tariffs even after voters in this month’s midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats. About two-thirds of voters said that Trump’s policies had made the economy worse, according to The AP Voter Poll, a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states. Trump has promised that the import taxes will bring back manufacturing jobs and reduce the federal deficit, but last year’s tariffs contributed to higher inflation that angered voters and led to calls by Democratic lawmakers to require congressional approval going forward. Greer said he did not expect the tariffs to rattle the global economy. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this -- they know what we’re proposing,” Greer told CNBC. “I think a lot of this is baked in.” The administration will next seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing Jan. 25, suggesting the duties won’t take effect until February or March. Tariffs may be here to stay despite electoral sweep Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the Finance Committee next year, said he will “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos.” “This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs,” Wyden added. “Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution.” Still, any effort to overturn them faces steep odds, even after Democrats take control of both chambers in January. Some Democrats will likely support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. And Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes. The small business advocacy group We Pay the Tariffs, which urged Congress to roll back all tariffs after the election, slammed Wednesday’s maneuver. “Three weeks ago, voters unambiguously rejected tariffs that have worsened the affordability crisis and devastated small businesses,” Dan Anthony, executive director of the group, said in a prepared statement. “Customers can’t afford more price increases, but small businesses can’t afford to absorb tariffs on top of tariffs either.” Brazil and China will face some of the biggest hits The levies will be imposed pursuant to Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which permits the president to impose import taxes and other sanctions against countries found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. The administration said the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes. Brazil was singled out for extra punishment after trade talks stalled. The U.S. is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10 per cent tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker. Brazil’s government expressed indignation over the proposed tariffs and threatened retaliatory measures. “The USTR’s unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process,” it said in a statement. “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat.” It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products.” For some Chinese goods, the new 20 per cent tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45 per cent. The U.S. and China last year reached a trade truce that is set to expire on Jan. 10, 2027. Greer told CNBC that the administration is proposing a “broad exemption” for US$30 billion worth of Chinese goods in line with the truce. Trump met last week in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and plans to host him next month at the Group of 20 summit in Florida, an event at which the truce and issues over access to rare earth minerals and China’s purchases of American agricultural products could come up again. On Wednesday, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs again stated its opposition while calling for the U.S. to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said. Some analysts criticized the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices. China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined,” said Derek Scissors, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour.” The tariffs won’t stack on top of other taxes on cars and steel Goldman Sachs calculates that the proposal would return most tariffs on the affected countries to where they were before the U.S. Supreme Court ruling in February. Goldman also estimates that if implemented, the import taxes would increase the overall U.S. tariff rate from 7.8 per cent to 9.2 per cent and have “a very small incremental impact” on inflation. The new import taxes are targeted to specific products and would not stack on top of separate tariffs on automobiles, steel, aluminum and other products that the administration has separately imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962. Nor would they stack on top of levies of 10 per cent to 12.5 per cent announced in July for 60 trading partners that the White House said have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labour. Other nations facing the new tariffs are Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam. Two other countries face pending investigations: Mexico and Norway. The USTR posted extensive reports on each country’s alleged unfair trade practices, with the report on China reaching 456 pages. The Section 301 law requires specific analysis of each country’s trade practices to pass legal muster. Wednesday’s duties will likely face legal challenges, as Trump’s forced labour tariffs already have. At least some of the forced labour duties could be overturned, said Ryan Majerus, a trade lawyer and former official in Trump’s first term who also served in the Biden administration, because the USTR didn’t provide extensive evidence for each of the 60 countries affected by those duties. ------ By Christopher Rugaber, Aamer Madhani and Josh Boak AP writers Mae Anderson in New York City and Huizhong Wu in Bangkok contributed to this report.

'Why Now?': Daniel Newman Warns Trump's Tariff Plans Could Fuel Inflation and Delay Interest Rate Cuts
The Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman says higher import costs could pressure consumers, businesses and financial markets as Washington weighs new trade measures
Daniel Newman, CEO of The Futurum Group, warned on Tuesday, 24 November 2026, that Trump's tariff plans could fuel inflation in the US and delay interest rate cuts.
The technology analyst questioned whether higher import duties were compatible with President Donald Trump's economic ambitions.
The Trump administration initially pursued investigations involving China, the European Union and 14 other economies.
The move follows a 20 February Supreme Court ruling that found the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not authorise the president to impose tariffs.
Trump's Tariff Plans Could Complicate Federal Reserve Rate Decisions
Writing on X, Newman questioned the economic rationale behind the proposed tariff increases, particularly given Trump's preference for lower borrowing costs.
According to Benzinga, Newman expressed concern that renewed trade restrictions could put financial markets under pressure.
'It will make the case for higher inflation and further FED hawkishness,' Newman wrote.
Companies that pass additional import costs on to consumers could contribute to inflation, while businesses absorbing those expenses may face narrower profit margins.
Persistent inflation could make the Federal Reserve more reluctant to reduce interest rates, potentially prolonging higher borrowing costs for households and businesses.
However, tariffs do not necessarily produce sustained inflation. Federal Reserve policymakers also consider employment conditions, consumer spending and broader economic indicators when determining interest rates.
Newman questioned what negotiating advantage Washington hoped to secure through additional tariffs following previous legal challenges.
'Why now?' he asked.
His warning represents an economic assessment rather than a confirmed forecast of the Federal Reserve's next policy decision.
White House Pursues Higher Tariffs Despite Republican Midterm Losses
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer launched investigations in March under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The investigations examined foreign industrial policies, including subsidies that Washington believes disadvantage American manufacturers.
Bloomberg reported in August that Washington was considering an increase of 7.5 percentage points on Chinese imports, potentially raising Trump's second-term tariff rate to 20 per cent.
In a subsequent update on 25 November, Reuters reported that Washington had proposed new tariffs affecting 14 trading partners.
Tariff ceilings for the European Union, Japan and South Korea are expected to remain at 15 per cent under existing trade arrangements. Older product-specific duties may also apply.
The proposals indicate that Republican electoral setbacks on 3 November have not substantially altered the administration's approach to trade policy.
Speaking at the B20 summit in Washington on 10 November, White House Office of Public Liaison Director Jim Goyer indicated that the administration's tariff campaign was 'just getting started'.
The proposed measures remain subject to further procedures before implementation.
US-China Trade Truce Faces Renewed Uncertainty
The prospect of higher American tariffs coincides with Beijing's efforts to preserve temporary trade concessions.
On 9 November, China's Ministry of Finance announced a two-month extension of its suspension of an additional 24 per cent tariff on American imports.
The suspension runs until 10 January 2027, while an additional 10 per cent tariff remains in place.
Reuters previously reported that negotiations over reciprocal tariff reductions, including concessions involving American agricultural products, had yet to produce a final agreement.
On 24 November, China's Ministry of Commerce announced that certain export restrictions would remain suspended until 27 January 2027.
The suspension covers dual-use items involving gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials.
It also includes enhanced end-user and end-use reviews for US-bound graphite shipments, although other applicable export controls may remain in force.
The extension provides temporary relief for American importers as Washington and Beijing navigate continuing disagreements over trade policy and industrial competition.

sources.news_title: Trump proposes new tariffs on 14 partners including Singapore, Malaysia and China
sources.text:
WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump reignited global trade tensions on Wednesday (Nov 25) by proposing new tariffs on major trading powers including a 20 per cent tariff on Singapore.
His administration proposed levies on 14 trading partners to combat what it calls structural excess industrial capacity. The highest rate of 20 per cent would hit China, which Washington blames for flooding world markets with cheap exports of everything from steel to electric vehicles and solar products.
"We know that they don't like these actions, but we are seeking stability with the Chinese. China is seeking stability with us," a senior US official said, adding Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping last week was "really great".
Beijing earlier reiterated its opposition to "trade wars" and dismissed the notion of overcapacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.
"The so-called 'overcapacity' is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said, urging the world's two top economies to maintain stable relations.
The senior US official said the administration also proposed tariffs on Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. For now, Mexico and Norway are excluded from new levies.
The new duties will take into account any trade deals agreed with the Trump administration and will not stack on top of some previous tariff rounds, suggesting many countries may not see a massive increase in the trading cost with the US.
Even so, the prospect of new trade burdens weighed on stock markets on Wednesday as a tech-led rally continued to run out of steam. MSCI's gauge of stocks around the globe fell 0.5 per cent.
"It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind," ING analysts wrote.
Proposed tariffs on Singapore
In a statement posted on the website of the office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR), the proposed rate for Singapore is up to 20 per cent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, on all goods of Singapore, with exemption for certain goods.
"The Trade Representative further proposes to consider adjusting the tariff rate applied to each good to 10 percent to account for any commitments in the event that Singapore were to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States, or conclude other negotiations that are responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies, and practices of Singapore," the statement read.
A separate investigation report accompanying its statement alleged that Singapore engages in acts, policies, and practices that create, sustain, or contribute to structural excess capacity and production.
This, it claimed, is created by maintaining a disproportionately large manufacturing sector, promoting production and exports, and failing to effectively address global structural excess capacity.
According to the USTR, such actions, policies and practices burden or restrict US commerce by reducing commercial opportunities for its producers and exporters in Singapore and third-country markets; harming the US economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in its manufacturing sector; and increasing US economic security risks.
AsiaOne has reached out to the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry for its comments on the claims made in the USTR's report and the proposed tariff rate.
New duties won't exceed negotiated limits
Trump's tariffs have contributed to higher prices on consumer goods in the United States, and a Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll following November's midterm losses for his Republicans showed 62 per cent of respondents would support efforts to repeal them.
But Trump has long served notice of a plan to rebuild the duties the US Supreme Court struck down in February. The latest ones come after an eight-month Section 301 unfair trade practices probe.
The US official also said the new duties would not exceed tariff limits in any trade deals with the Trump administration, including a 20 per cent cap for China during Trump's second term under a year-old truce with Beijing that is due to expire on Jan 10.
The tariffs would also not apply to about US$30 billion (S$39 billion) worth of Chinese imports that the US is considering for tariff reductions under a bilateral process, the official said.
However, they would add to the tariffs on China put in place during Trump's first term, which amounted to roughly 25 per cent.
The proposed duties will further not stack on top of tariffs of 10 per cent or 12.5 per cent that the administration imposed in July on a wider group of 60 trading partners over allegations of lax enforcement of anti-forced-labor laws. Specific rates are to be published in a US Federal Register notice on Wednesday.
Tariff rates also will be consistent with trade agreements signed by other partners, the official said, including the 15 per cent cap agreed by the EU, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, as well as a 19 per cent cap agreed by Malaysia.
The proposed duties will be subject to a public notice and comment period, with a hearing scheduled before they go into effect. The official said that could push implementation into January.
Additional reporting by AsiaOne

sources.news_title: US proposes new tariffs on trading partners, including EU
sources.text:
The US has unveiled proposed tariffs on 14 economies, including the European Union and China, after a months long probe into alleged excess production - the latest move by US President Donald Trump to remake Washington's trade relationships.
The US Trade Representative's (USTR) office announced the duties after completing an eight-month Section 301 unfair trade practices probe into 16 trading partners, including close allies Japan, the European Union and South Korea.
For the time being, the USTR did not propose tariffs on goods from Mexico and Norway.
A senior US official said that tariffs were proposed for goods from China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.
The specific rates were to be published in a US Federal Register notice.
The official said Washington had concluded that each of those trading partners "creates, sustains, or contributes to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors through various acts, policies and practices that we find to be unreasonable and burden or restrict US commerce".
USTR defines structural excess capacity as situations where countries "are promoting production and capacity divorced from the realities of demand and market principles", the official said, including through the use of industrial policies, subsidies and the use of components imported from non-market economies.
RTÉ's Europe Editor Tony Connelly reports on the implications for the EU

EU expects US to honour 15% tarriff deal
The EU said that it rejected the premise of new tariffs on its exports and expected Washington to stick by a deal struck with Brussels last year.
"We will study the findings," European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said.
"At the same time we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity," he said.
"The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action."
The Commission would continue engaging with Washington on implementing a tariff deal struck in 2025 to cap Trump's duties on the bloc at 15%, he added.
"We expect any measure from this investigation to respect it in full, including when combined with existing duties," Mr Gill said.
Outcome does not put any new tariffs for EU in place, McEntee says
The Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade Helen McEntee welcomed progress towards a US tariff exemption for Irish whiskey.
She said she will discuss the matters with EU Commissioner for Trade Maroš Šefčovič and fellow trade ministers at a scheduled Foreign Affairs Council Trade meeting next Monday.
"We are still examining the details of the announcement, and our initial assessment is that the outcome of the investigation respects the agreement reached between President von der Leyen and President Trump in Turnberry last year," she said.
"The outcome today does not put any new tariffs in place but are open for further public comment. For now, the current tariff of 10% on goods from the EU remains in place, unless otherwise exempted."
The Minister described it as "positive" that Irish whiskey is listed in the part II annex which outlines goods not covered by the proposed action.
"Our ambition is to ensure reduced tariffs in other key areas such as MedTech and the technology sectors," she said.
China to face highest tariffs of 14 trading partners, US official says
China would face the highest tariff rates of the 14 trading partners as the proposed 20% excess capacity tariffs on Chinese goods would be in addition to the roughly 25% tariffs imposed during Mr Trump's first term in office, the US official said.
The official added that this would keep China above the 20% proposed rate for Vietnam.
The new tariffs will not stack on top of those sector-specific tariffs on items like automobiles and steel, the senior US official said.
In July, Mr Trump imposed a separate wave of tariffs on 60 economies, accusing them of insufficient action against forced labour.
For economies facing both the forced labour and excess production tariffs, the levies would not stack, the US official said.
Instead, the higher rate of the two would prevail.
Those duties and the excess-capacity tariffs are widely viewed as rebuilding Mr Trump's global tariffs that were struck down in February by the US Supreme Court.
The US official said the new duties would not exceed tariff limits in trade deals negotiated by the Trump administration, including a 20% cap for China during Mr Trump's second term under a year-old trade truce with Beijing that is due to expire on 10 January.
The tariffs would not apply to about $30 billion (€27 billion) worth of Chinese imports that the US is considering for tariff reductions under a bilateral process, called the Board of Trade, the official said.
The official said Washington did not expect China to retaliate against the new excess-capacity duties.
"We know that they don't like these actions, but we are seeking stability with the Chinese. China is seeking stability with us," the official said.
Mr Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping last week was "really great" and that there was progress on supplies of Chinese rare earth minerals in recent days, the official added.
But the US determination is likely to face strong pushback from China and others, with Beijing long rejecting criticism that it relies too much on exports to boost its economy.
Tariff rates also will be consistent with trade agreements signed by other partners, the official said, including the 15% cap agreed by the EU, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, as well as a 19% cap agreed by Malaysia.
But several countries, such as India and Vietnam, do not have finalised trade deals.
The US official said that the new duties were expected to result in more trade agreements being negotiated and finalised, possibly at a G20 leaders' summit in Miami in December.
The proposed duties will be subject to a public notice and comment period, with a hearing scheduled before they go into effect.
The official said that could push implementation into January.
USTR was still reviewing excess capacity probes into Norway and Mexico, the official said, declining to provide a timeline for their completion.
US officials briefed congressional committees on the changes late yesterday.
Affected countries were also notified, the official said.
In a separate announcement, the US Trade Representative's office also proposed additional tariffs on goods from Brazil, including aircraft, over alleged inaction on addressing US trade concerns.
Over-capacity concerns affect a range of sectors, from batteries to cement, chemicals to processed food, the senior US official said.
The duties could add further pressure on US businesses already squeezed by earlier tariffs, with firms now likelier to pass on costs to consumers already frustrated with the high cost of living.
Affordability was a key issue in recent midterm elections, which saw President Trump's Republican Party swept out of power in both houses of Congress by Democrats.
US consumer inflation came in at 3.7% year-on-year in September, close to a three-year high as prices are pushed up by the effects of Mr Trump's war on Iran, tariffs and the massive AI investment boom.
US Federal Reserve policymakers, responsible for keeping inflation to a long-term two-percent target, say that most price effects of Mr Trump's previous tariff rollout have passed through the economy.
However, they said any new levies could push prices up further.
A Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll following November's midterm elections showed 62% of respondents would support efforts to repeal the tariffs.
The new tariffs are likely to come into effect in January at the earliest, the senior US official said.
The Trump administration has singled out China as the biggest source of excess industrial capacity, which it says is flooding global markets with steel, aluminum, electric vehicles, appliances, solar products and other goods.
China has rejected the accusations, saying its exports reflect competitive advantages.
The probe was also partly directed at Chinese investment in countries in southeast Asia, including Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia, which Washington says is used to manufacture goods for the US market and avoid prior US tariffs.

sources.news_title: Trump administration to introduce new tariffs on China, EU and other major trading partners
sources.text:
Trump administration to introduce new tariffs on China, EU and 12 other major trading partners
The Trump administration said it will issue a new wave of tariffs on China and other major U.S. trading partners, the latest escalation in global trade tensions.
The U.S. will increase tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20%, raising the total tariff rate on the world's second-largest economy to 45%. President Trump also plans to raise taxes on specific products from the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan and India.
Brazil is among the countries that will be hardest hit, with the U.S. planning to raise tariffs on the country's raw and refined sugar and to impose a new 10% levy on aircraft.
The planned tariffs are meant to curtail trade practices that the U.S. says undercut American companies, including what the White House has called excessive manufacturing output from those economies.
"For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America's manufacturing base,"  U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer 
said in a statement.
The planned duties would be imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which authorizes the USTR to investigate trade agreements if they violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces, or actively discriminate against American goods.
The announcement came after the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) completed a series of months-long investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and Taiwan. The USTR is also investigating Mexico and Norway but hasn't imposed any new tariffs on those countries.
In a call with reporters late Tuesday, a senior administration official said the tariffs are in the proposal phase and did not provide an implementation timeline. The official stressed that the tariffs are targeted at specific products and would not be stacked on top of existing tariffs introduced by the Trump administration.
Stephen Brown, chief North American economist for Capital Economics, said in a research note Wednesday that the Trump administration's announcement is "not as alarming as it looks." The new tariffs will essentially replace previously announced Section 301 tariffs, rather than stacking on top of them, he said.
Tariffs have been a central part of the Trump administration's economic agenda, with the president arguing they are necessary to boost U.S. manufacturing, create jobs and reduce the trade deficit. However, his authority to impose the levies has faced legal challenges, complicating the rollout.
Tariffs unpopular with voters, small businesses
In February, the Supreme Court blocked a sweeping set of tariffs that the president implemented in 2025 under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, dismantling a key part of the administration's efforts and forcing the government to issue refunds to thousands of affected businesses.
Still, the administration has found other avenues to impose the levies, using other sections of trade law, such as Section 232, which allows the president to restrict imports that could threaten U.S. national security.
The average statutory U.S. tariff rate on imports is now 11.2%, according to the Yale Budget Lab.
The White House moved to propose the new tariffs on Wednesday despite mounting frustration among U.S. voters over rising costs. In a CBS News poll conducted after the midterms, 66% of respondents said President Trump's tariffs have hurt the national economy.
Tariffs are taxes on imported goods. They raise costs for businesses, which sometimes pass the burden onto consumers in the form of higher prices.
We Pay the Tariffs, a grassroots coalition of small businesses, decried the new tariffs, warning they could raise prices just as the holiday season heats up.
"Three weeks ago, voters unambiguously rejected tariffs that have worsened the affordability crisis and devastated small businesses," Dan Anthony, executive director of We Pay the Tariffs, said in a statement. "Customers can't afford more price increases, but small businesses can't afford to absorb tariffs on top [of] tariffs either."

sources.news_title: Trump Proposes Tariffs of Up to 35% on 14 Trading Partners, but Not Before January
sources.text:
Trump Proposes Tariffs of Up to 35% on 14 Trading Partners, but Not Before January
The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed new tariffs of up to 35% on goods from 14 trading partners, including China, the European Union, and Japan, but none would take effect before public hearings set for late January.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer found that the 14 economies’ policies that build “structural excess capacity” in manufacturing are unreasonable and burden U.S. commerce under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, his office said.
The proposed top rates, according to the trade representative’s office, are:
- Vietnam: up to 35%, or 20% if it reaches a trade deal
- India: up to 25%, or 17% with a deal
- China: up to 20% on most goods and 10% on some others
- Singapore: up to 20%
- Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand: up to 18%
- European Union: 15%
- Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, and Taiwan: up to 15%
Mexico and Norway, which were part of the original 16-economy probe CDN reported Tuesday, got no determination for now, the office said.
What It Could Mean for Prices
Greer said most rates are “not really additive” and generally won’t stack on existing duties. “When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points,” he told CNBC.
China is the exception. A senior official said its 20% rate would come on top of first-term tariffs of roughly 25%, putting duties on Chinese goods near 45%, CNBC reported.
For every country but China, the proposals exempt goods already hit by Section 232 tariffs, including steel, aluminum, copper, cars, light trucks, auto parts, wood products, patented drugs, and semiconductors, according to a LexBlog summary of the notices.
The tariffs would also skip about $30 billion of Chinese imports that the two countries are weighing for tariff cuts, Reuters reported.
The administration’s tariffs have contributed in part to higher consumer prices, and 62% of Americans in a post-midterm Reuters/Ipsos poll would support efforts to repeal them, Reuters reported.
When It Could Start
Written comments and requests to testify are due Jan. 5, 2027, and hearings begin Jan. 25, the trade office said.
“I don’t think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now,” Greer told CNBC.
The China rate stays within the 20% cap in a trade truce with Beijing that expires Jan. 10, a U.S. official said, Reuters reported.
China rejected the premise. “The so-called ‘overcapacity’ does not really exist,” its foreign ministry said, according to CNBC.
Greer said trading partners have used “wage and labor suppression,” subsidies, and other practices “that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America’s manufacturing base,” his office said.
Stocks fell as investors weighed the tariffs alongside hotter inflation and a slide in AI shares. The S&P 500 was down 2.2% around noon Eastern, the Associated Press reported.
Core prices in the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge rose 3.3% from a year earlier in October, above the 3.2% forecast, Yahoo Finance reported. Markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving and reopen Friday for a half day.

The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed a fresh round of tariffs targeting 14 US trading partners, among them China, Japan, India and the European Union.
The targeted countries have excessive manufacturing capacity that hurting US businesses, a senior US official told reporters late Tuesday.
China faces an additional 20% levy that could rise to 40% if Beijing fails to honor its trade truce with Washington. Levies on most of the other trade partners are expected to come in at the 10% to 18% range.
