US proposes new tariffs on 14 partners, including China and the EU
sources.text:
The US proposed new tariffs on 14 trading partners on Wednesday. China, the European Union, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan are on the list. The Trump administration says the duties target “structural excess capacity”, meaning factory output that subsidies keep high and that undercuts US manufacturers.
The US Trade Representative’s office announced the tariffs after an eight-month Section 301 investigation into 16 economies. David Lawder and Andrea Shalal reported the details for Reuters, citing a senior US official.
The other nine economies are Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam. The US spared Mexico and Norway, the last two economies in the investigation, for now. USTR planned to publish the exact rates in the Federal Register on Wednesday.
China faces the highest rate
China would face a 20% tariff on most of its imports, Courtenay Brown reported for Axios. That comes on top of the roughly 25% tariffs from Trump’s first term, according to Reuters. For some Chinese goods, the total rate would reach 45%, according to AP.
A senior US official told Axios the rate could rise to 40% if trade talks break down or China fails to meet its commitments. The 20% rate stays within the cap set by the trade truce with Beijing, which expires on 10 January, Reuters reported. About $30bn of Chinese imports under review for tariff cuts would be exempt.
“We know that they don’t like these actions, but we are seeking stability with the Chinese. China is seeking stability with us,” the senior US official said, according to Reuters.
The new tariffs will not surprise Beijing and are unlikely to undermine the truce, the official said, AP reported.
China’s foreign ministry rejected the idea of overcapacity but stopped short of threatening retaliation, Reuters reported.
“The so-called ‘overcapacity’ is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation,” foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.
The other 13
For the others, the proposals mostly target specific goods. They would raise existing tariffs by about 5 percentage points on average, the official told Axios. They would also stay within the caps in Trump’s trade deals: 15% for the EU, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, and 19% for Malaysia, according to Reuters.
Vietnam faces a rate of up to 35%, while others face 20% or 25%, the BBC reported. Caps in Trump’s trade deals will lower some of those rates, the BBC said.
The new duties will not stack on top of the 10% and 12.5% forced-labour tariffs the US put on 60 trading partners in July. Nor will they stack on the separate tariffs on cars, steel and aluminium, AP reported.
USTR’s notice pointed to unprofitable carmakers in China and Japan, according to Reuters’ live coverage. For the EU, it cited Germany’s and Ireland’s large goods surpluses with the US.
The duties are not final. They face a public comment period and a hearing, and may not take effect until January, the official told Reuters.
Brazil, voters and the markets
The US singled out Brazil after trade talks stalled, AP reported. It proposed higher tariffs on raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, which would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.
The plan replaces broader tariffs that the Supreme Court struck down in February. It also follows Republican losses in this month’s midterm elections. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll after the vote, 62% of respondents said they would support efforts to repeal Trump’s tariffs, Reuters reported.
Asian stocks fell sharply on Wednesday as reports of the plan added to worries about the tech sector, Semafor reported. MSCI’s global stock index fell 0.5%, according to Reuters.
The announcement follows Trump’s summit in Shenzhen with Xi Jinping last week. Trump plans to host Xi next month at the G20 summit in Florida, AP reported.
The new duties sit alongside the existing US semiconductor tariff. Earlier this month, Trump said he would tax US companies that build data centres abroad.

sources.news_title: US plans to hike tariffs on several countries, including additional 20% on China - American Press
sources.text:
US plans to hike tariffs on several countries, including additional 20% on China
|                            Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...                        | 
President Donald Trump’s administration is planning to hike tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20% and raise import taxes on products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.
The new tariffs proposed on Wednesday are meant to discourage excessive factory output in those economies, boosted by subsidies and other trade barriers that the Republican administration says put American manufacturers at a disadvantage. The taxes are also intended to help replace the tariff revenues lost after the Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.
The new tariffs stem from investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he did not expect the tariffs to rattle the global economy.
“We’ve talked to our trading partners about this — they know what we’re proposing,” Greer told CNBC. “I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don’t think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now.”
The tariffs, rolled out the day before Thanksgiving, represent another controversial twist in Trump’s economic policy. Voters in this month’s midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats, with about two-thirds of voters saying that Trump’s policies had made the economy worse, according to The AP Voter Poll, a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states.
Trump has promised that the import taxes will bring back manufacturing jobs and reduce the federal deficit, but last year’s tariffs contributed to higher inflation that angered voters and led to calls by Democratic lawmakers to require congressional approval going forward.
Brazil and China will face some of the biggest hits
The Trump administration is arguing that these countries’ industrial policies have undercut American companies, contributing to a trade deficit in goods that has recently exceeded $1 trillion annually.
The legal basis of the planned tariffs is Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which enables the U.S. government to investigate and retaliate against foreign trade practices that violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces or actively discriminate against American goods. A senior Trump administration official told reporters that the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes.
Brazil was separately singled out Wednesday for extra punishment after talks on trade issues stalled. The U.S. is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a move that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.
For some Chinese goods, the new 20% tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.
Like China, Vietnam also faces a 20% rate, pending finalization of trade talks, the USTR said on Wednesday. The tariffs for other trading partners range from 10% to 18%.
The U.S. and China last year reached a trade truce that is set to expire on Jan. 10, 2027. Greer told CNBC that the administration is proposing a “broad exemption” for $30 billion worth of Chinese goods in line with the truce.
Trump met last week in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and plans to host him next month at the Group of 20 summit in Florida, an event at which the truce and issues over access to rare earth minerals and China’s purchases of American agricultural products could be discussed again.
China has pushed back consistently on U.S. tariffs. On Wednesday, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs again stated its opposition while calling for the U.S. to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said. “The so-called overcapacity is a false narrative, and China opposes using it as a pretext for political manipulation.”

sources.news_title: US proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners to fight excess factory ...
Trump targets China in new round of tariffs
sources.text:
President Donald Trump is preparing to impose a new round of tariffs on China and dozens of other countries, seeking to revive his trade agenda after the Supreme Court struck down the sweeping global tariffs he introduced earlier this year.
China and Vietnam are set to face a 20% tariff, the highest proposed rate among the 14 trading partners targeted by the investigation. Rates could go even higher if countries don’t adhere to pre-existing trade agreements. For China, it could rise to 40%, and for Vietnam, 35%.
Meanwhile, the European Union’s proposed starting rate would be 15%, but it could go up to 20%.
The earliest the administration expects the tariffs to take effect is January, the official said. Before imposing the tariffs, the administration must complete a public notice-and-comment process and hold hearings, the official said.
The proposal calls for broad exclusions for energy, food that can’t easily be grown in the US, certain semiconductor chips and pharmaceuticals. Additionally, they would not stack with existing duties on products such as automobiles, steel and aluminum.
Americans are unlikely to see prices rise substantially from the tariff changes, in part because of the exclusions, but also since businesses have already factored these rates, which mirror prior levels, into pricing.
These latest tariffs stem from a monthslong investigation undertaken by the Office of the US Trade Representative into whether foreign governments are incentivizing excess manufacturing through measures like subsidies, and favorable loan terms. The administration argues this allows foreign companies to produce more than they otherwise would and then sell at artificially low prices, undercutting their American competitors.
The White House official said he believes retaliation will be limited and noted that trading partners received advanced notice of the proposed actions.
The announcement comes after Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping struck a notably friendly tone during their recent meeting. Trump, meanwhile, took credit for getting Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO on Monday, despite bipartisan concerns around whether China is using advanced Nvidia chips to bolster its military capabilities by bypassing export restrictions.
Post-election maneuver
With the bruising midterm elections behind them, Trump officials appear keen on turning their attention back to the president’s trade agenda.
That’s unlikely to score well with voters and some Republican lawmakers.
Two-thirds of voters said Trump’s tariffs hurt the national economy, according to nationwide results of CNN’s Voter Poll. Nearly the same share said they hurt the local economy, too.
Voters took their frustration with Trump’s tariffs to the polls in the midterms, electing an unprecedented number of Democrats, many of whom hail from historically Republican states and districts.
Since the election, a growing number of Republicans, including Sens. Ted Cruz and Todd Young, have publicly raised concerns about Trump’s tariff policies. Their opposition could present a growing obstacle to the president’s trade agenda if they join Democrats in challenging it.
“One of the causes of increased costs is that our current tariff structure is overly broad, and as a result, it is negatively affecting too many American factory floors, farms, small businesses, and family budgets,” Young said in a post on X after the midterm elections. “I’ve said for over a year that our tariff policy must be tied to clear objectives focused on protecting America’s economic and national security.”

sources.news_title: US plans to hike tariffs on China, EU, Brazil and others over subsidized production
U.S. proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU
sources.text:
The U.S. is preparing new tariffs on 14 economies, including China, the EU, Japan and India, following investigations into what the Trump administration says are excess manufacturing practices that disadvantage U.S. commerce.
The administration launched those and other trade investigations in March, weeks after the Supreme Court unraveled a major piece of President Donald Trump's tariff-heavy economic policy by striking down his "liberation day" duties. Trump has since been accused by critics of his tariffs of trying to revive the canceled duties using other legal authorities.
The latest action targets foreign economies that create, sustain or contribute to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors that the U.S. finds unreasonable and burdensome or restrictive to its commerce, a senior U.S. official told reporters Tuesday evening.
The new tariffs are "targeted," not blanket rates, and will vary for each economy, and many will not exceed the rates established in previously reached trade deals, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the forthcoming duties.
The rates, which mostly range from 15% to 20%, are "not really additive" and generally will not stack on top of existing duties, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" Wednesday morning.
"In effect, it'll look more like a top up," Greer said. "When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points."
An exception is China, which faces a 20% rate under the new tariff policy, "so it will go up some," Greer said. But at the same time, both countries are moving to remove tariffs on some of each other's goods in what Greer called "stability-generating activity through this action."
The senior U.S. official said Tuesday that the 20% rate will come on top of the so-called forced technology transfer-related tariffs of roughly 25%, which were implemented during Trump's first presidential term. U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods will therefore reach about 45%, give or take for different goods, the official said.
Average U.S. tariffs rates on Chinese goods stood at about 36.5% as of July, according to the Congressional Research Service.
Greer also said on CNBC that the new policy likely will not take effect for months.
"We've talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing," he said. "I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don't think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now."
The administration says the tariffs target what it calls "overcapacity" — excess industrial production, often supported by government subsidies, that allows cheaper goods to flood global markets and undercut U.S. producers.
China has disputed the allegations. "The so-called 'overcapacity' does not really exist," China's foreign ministry said Wednesday before the official reports were released by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, according to Reuters.
The overcapacity levies are being imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The Trump administration invoked the same statute to launch investigations into 60 economies over alleged forced-labor issues.
Those investigations, which also began in March, led to broad tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on goods from dozens of countries covering 99.4% of U.S. imports.
The Section 301 actions came weeks after the Supreme Court struck down the near-global tariffs that Trump had enacted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.
Shortly after the court's ruling, Trump invoked Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 to impose a 10% global tariff. That tariff expired after 150 days, and was immediately replaced with the forced-labor-related duties.
An ongoing lawsuit accuses the Trump administration of citing forced-labor issues as a "pretext" in pursuit of reviving Trump's worldwide tariff regime.

sources.news_title: US unveils proposed tariffs on major partners, including EU and China
US proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including rate of up to 20% for Singapore
sources.text:
US proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including rate of up to 20% for Singapore
China faces the highest levies; Mexico and Norway are spared for now
[WASHINGTON] US President Donald Trump fired a new tariff salvo on Wednesday (Nov 25) on 14 major trading partners including China, Japan and the EU, undeterred in his protectionist push by the losses his Republican Party suffered in US midterm elections.
His administration proposed new maximum potential rates of 20 to 40 per cent to counter excess industrial capacity that it says these countries are promoting.
But the US Trade Representative’s (USTR) office said it intends to cap new tariffs at lower levels agreed under trade deals that are completed or still under negotiation.
In unveiling the results of an eight-month unfair trade practices investigation into excess industrial capacity, USTR aims to more fully rebuild Trump’s tariff leverage after the Supreme Court in February struck down his broad global duties under a national emergencies law.
The effort also seeks to put Trump’s tariffs and associated trade agreements on more solid legal and political grounds by backing them with a court-tested trade law, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, and addressing foreign subsidies and industrial policies that are viewed as major trade problems by both Republicans and Democrats.
Separately, USTR proposed a new 10 per cent tariff on imports of Brazil’s finished Embraer commercial aircraft, and an increase in duties on imports of Brazilian sugar that exceed quotas as part of an effort to push Brasilia to rectify alleged unfair trade practices.
The products were previously exempted from Trump’s 25 per cent tariffs on Brazilian goods that were imposed in July under a separate Section 301 investigation.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he decided to propose the tariff increases after months of talks between the US and Brazil made “no meaningful progress”.
China tops excess capacity rates
Under the excess factory capacity probe, USTR said China would face the highest capped rate of 20 per cent, which would be added to duties of roughly 25 per cent imposed during Trump’s first term.
That rate would comply with a US-China trade truce that expires on Jan 10. But if the truce unravels, China’s rate would rise to 40 per cent, the USTR said.
Vietnam would face a capped tariff rate of 20 per cent if it reaches a trade agreement with Washington, rising to 35 per cent if negotiations fail.
Greer said the tariffs, which would not take effect until after a Jan 25 public hearing, were intended to counteract “industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labour suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices” that undermine the US manufacturing base.
The duties would not stack on top of prior tariffs of 10 per cent or 12.5 per cent imposed under a separate US probe into lax enforcement of anti-forced labour laws in 60 economies, nor would they add to sectoral national security duties on steel, aluminum, autos and other goods.
Greer said the proposed tariffs also would not apply to about US$30 billion of Chinese imports under consideration for tariff reductions through a bilateral mechanism known as the Board of Trade.
Washington has long accused China of subsidising industry and flooding global markets with low-cost exports ranging from steel to electric vehicles and solar products.
A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China is a source of excess capacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.
“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Lower rates for trade deals
The USTR also proposed capped tariff rates of 18 per cent for imported goods from Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Bangladesh, and 15 per cent, including existing “Most Favoured Nation” duties, for Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, the EU and Switzerland.
India, which has yet to reach a trade deal with the Trump administration, would face a 17 per cent tariff rate if an agreement is finalised and a 25 per cent rate if talks fail, the USTR said. The proposed tariff on Singapore would not exceed 20 per cent, but could fall to 10 per cent if an agreement is reached or negotiations succeed.
Greer told CNBC the proposed caps were consistent with trade agreements reached over the past year that also lowered barriers to US exports.
“We’re sticking to that in terms of our proposals because we think a lot of these deals we made actually solve a lot of the problems we see in excess capacity or can go towards it,” Greer said, adding that the capped rates are no surprise to trading partners.
Mexico and Norway were excluded from the proposals because investigations into their trade practices remain under way, Greer said.
Even so, the prospect of new trade barriers weighed on stock markets on Wednesday amid a renewed sell-off in tech stocks. Major US indices opened down more than 1 per cent, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite down more than 3 per cent.
“It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind,” ING analysts wrote.
More support, durability
Trump’s tariffs and their impact on rising living costs were a major issue in Democrats’ sweeping victory in midterm elections.
A Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll conducted after Republicans’ midterm losses found 62 per cent of respondents supported efforts by Democrats to repeal them.
US Senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat who is expected to chair the Senate Finance Committee when the new Congress begins in January, said: “Not even a month after voters rejected his disastrous trade agenda, Trump has decided to yet again increase prices for Americans. As Finance Committee chair, I will use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s disastrous tariffs.”
But that will not be easy, because there is bipartisan support in Congress for countering excess capacity largely centred in China, said Nathaniel Halvorson, a former USTR official who is now a trade partner at Baker Mckenzie.
Undoing the tariffs also could cause some trade deals to collapse, Halvorson said, and Democrats “would have to consider whether they want to undo a settlement that might be working for US interests to some extent”. REUTERS

sources.news_title: US plans to hike tariffs on China, EU, Brazil
sources.text:
President Donald Trump’s Administration is planning to hike tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20% and raise import taxes on products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.
The new tariffs proposed on Wednesday are meant to discourage excessive factory output in those economies, boosted by subsidies and other trade barriers that the Republican administration says put American manufacturers at a disadvantage.
The taxes are also intended to help replace the tariff revenues lost after the Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.
The new tariffs stem from investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he did not expect the tariffs to rattle the global economy.
“We’ve talked to our trading partners about this — they know what we’re proposing,” Greer told CNBC.
“I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don’t think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now.”
The tariffs, rolled out the day before Thanksgiving, represent another controversial twist in Trump’s economic policy.
Voters in this month’s midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats, with about two-thirds of voters saying that Trump’s policies had made the economy worse, according to The AP Voter Poll, a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states.
Trump has promised that the import taxes will bring back manufacturing jobs and reduce the federal deficit, but last year’s tariffs contributed to higher inflation that angered voters and led to calls by Democratic lawmakers to require congressional approval going forward.
The Trump Administration is arguing that these countries’ industrial policies have undercut American companies, contributing to a trade deficit in goods that has recently exceeded $1 trillion annually.
The legal basis of the planned tariffs is Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which enables the USngovernment to investigate and retaliate against foreign trade practices that violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces or actively discriminate against American goods.
A senior Trump administration official told reporters that the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes.
Brazil was separately singled out Wednesday for extra punishment after talks on trade issues stalled.
The US is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a move that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.
For some Chinese goods, the new 20% tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.
Like China, Vietnam also faces a 20% rate, pending finalisation of trade talks, the USTR said on Wednesday.
The tariffs for other trading partners range from 10% to 18%.
The USband China last year reached a trade truce that is set to expire on Jan. 10, 2027.
Greer told CNBC that the administration is proposing a “broad exemption” for $30 billion worth of Chinese goods in line with the truce.
Trump met last week in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and plans to host him next month at the Group of 20 summit in Florida, an event at which the truce and issues over access to rare earth minerals and China’s purchases of American agricultural products could be discussed again.

sources.news_title: Trump administration proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU
sources.text:
The United States is considering imposing new tariffs on 14 of its trading partners, including China and the European Union. According to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, the proposed measures could take effect in January next year.
The proposal calls for an additional 20% tariff on Chinese products, which would bring the overall tariff rate to around 40%.

The list of countries and regions also includes Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.
The measures are the result of an eight-month investigation by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, conducted under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The law allows the U.S. administration to take trade action against countries that, according to investigations, use unfair practices and harm U.S. trade.
U.S. authorities allege that the practices of the countries under investigation promote excess industrial capacity. They say subsidies, industrial policies and state support for domestic producers cause production to exceed market demand.
A senior U.S. official said that, according to Washington’s findings, these countries create or maintain excess production capacity through practices considered unreasonable that burden or restrict U.S. commerce.
China is expected to be hit hardest, with the additional 20% tariff. It would be added to tariffs of around 25% imposed during Trump’s first term, bringing the overall rate to more than 40% for some categories of goods.
However, the proposed tariffs would not automatically be added to all existing duties. The administration has said that implementation will respect the limits set out in trade agreements with partners. The agreed ceiling is 15% for the European Union, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, and 19% for Malaysia.
About $30 billion in imports from China, for which tariff reductions are being considered through a bilateral process, will be exempt from the proposed measures.
Before a final decision is made, the proposal will undergo public consultation and a hearing. The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative has scheduled the hearing for January 25. A U.S. official said the process could delay implementation of the tariffs until January 2027.
Mexico and Norway are not currently included on the list, as investigations into those two countries are ongoing.
The initiative comes several months after the U.S. Supreme Court, in February, struck down a significant portion of Trump’s sweeping tariffs, known as the “Liberation Day” tariffs.
The court ruled that the administration had exceeded its authority by relying on a national emergencies law to impose tariffs.
This time, the White House is using Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which establishes an investigative process for identifying and countering trade practices deemed unfair.
The Trump administration is therefore seeking to reinstate part of its tariff policy, but on a different legal basis.
Beijing has repeatedly rejected U.S. claims of excess industrial capacity, describing them as a pretext for political and trade measures.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun called the U.S. claims false.
“The so-called ‘overcapacity’ is a false claim, and China opposes its use as a pretext for political manipulation.”
Guo Jiakun urged Washington to maintain stable trade relations with Beijing.
The proposal comes as Trump’s tariff policy remains a central topic in the U.S. economic debate. The cost of imports and its consequences for American consumers also remain in the public spotlight.

India among 14 economies facing fresh tariffs

sources.text:
On the Dash:
- U.S.-China trade truce ends Jan. 10, and the US now proposes up to 20% on most Chinese goods.
- Reports say the new tariffs would not be added on top of car tariffs.
- China’s pause on new rare earth limits also ends Jan. 10, which matters for vehicle parts.
The Trump administration wants new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including up to 20% on most goods from China. The plan was released Wednesday by the U.S. Trade Representative’s office (USTR), citing these countries make more goods than they need and hurt U.S. factories.
The news comes weeks before the U.S.-China trade truce ends on Jan. 10, after a truce extended in September during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington. President Donald Trump met Xi again last week in Shenzhen at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
Former top Chinese trade negotiator Zhu Guangyao told Bloomberg TV that talks will resume in January. He expects progress, improved communication, and a fresh start in trade relations. He also said concerns raised by the U.S. overcapacity probe can be resolved through talks.
The new China tariff would sit on top of about 25% in tariffs from Trump’s first term. Japan, South Korea, the European Union and Taiwan would pay up to 15%. Vietnam would face up to 35% and India up to 25%. The plan isn’t final yet, and the public can comment before it takes effect.
Notably, the USTR named autos as an industry of concern in China, Japan, South Korea, and the EU. Reports say the new tariffs would not be added on top of the separate tariffs on cars, steel and aluminum. Those include the 25% Section 232 tariffs on imported vehicles and certain auto parts. It’s not clear yet which auto parts would be covered.
China’s Foreign Ministry said the claim is false and called the move political and did not threaten to hit back. A U.S. official said the plan is not likely to break the truce, and talks between the two sides are still set for January. Auto groups also want limits on Chinese automakers. Six trade groups, including dealers, urged Trump to keep those automakers out of the U.S. ahead of his September meeting with Xi.
For dealers, car tariffs stay under their own rules for now. The Jan. 10 date still matters for supply, because the truce includes a pause on new Chinese limits on rare earths. Those materials go into magnets used in EV and hybrid motors and many other vehicle parts. China’s earlier limits forced some automakers to stop work at some plants. SEC filings show GM ended a long-term magnet supply deal with a South Carolina plant, and the dispute is now in arbitration.
